paras: The Smithville shooting took place on Christmas Eve, December 24, 1880, at Smithville, Virginia, a hamlet on the road between Hampton and Yorktown, when a white farmer named Howard Dunn shot two Black men dead and stabbed others at a gathering called to organize a Black military company. Dunn surrendered, was tried in March 1881, and was acquitted. The wire story ran in papers across the country, and a later letter from Yorktown called the trial a sham.

Smithville, "more generally known as the 'Half-way House,'" lay fifteen miles west of Fortress Monroe. According to a fuller Fortress Monroe report, Dunn owned a large farm, had posted notices against hunting on it, and was said to have threatened to shoot trespassers. On the afternoon of December 24 a large crowd of Black men gathered at the Half-way House to organize a militia company.

The wire dispatch said one of the men caught Dunn by the whiskers and slapped his face, and that Dunn drew a single-barrelled pistol and killed him. The fuller report added that the men had been drinking and chaffing Dunn about his hunting notices, and said "it seemed to be the purpose of the negroes to provoke a fight." Dunn then retreated into a store and reloaded his pistol.

A crowd led by Dan Cook, who carried a sword as the company's prospective captain, entered the store, and Dunn shot Cook through the neck, killing him. Armed with a knife, Dunn cut his way out; Ed Drew was badly wounded in the abdomen and was expected to die, and another man was cut in the hand. Dunn went to the nearest magistrate, who, "fearing a reaction, and that a mob might be collected to lynch him," sent him under a deputy sheriff to the jail at Williamsburg.

A Chicago Tribune brief reported that Black men threatened to take Dunn from the jail and lynch him. In March 1881 the Clarke Courier reported that Dunn, "who killed Jasper Reed, colored," had been found not guilty at Hampton and released. Robert G. Guffin, writing from Yorktown, said the trial was held there before a substitute judge who had been a Confederate colonel and a jury of ex-Confederates.

Guffin wrote that Black residents held an indignation meeting on March 29 despite threats against its organizers, and appointed a committee to draft resolutions. He also said one stabbed man was still confined to his bed in April.

The first coverage was a short Fort Monroe dispatch of December 28, printed by the Richmond Dispatch as "Desperate Affray on the Peninsula" and by the Alexandria Gazette as "FATAL AFFRAY." Northern papers carried the same text under headlines such as "TWO NEGROES SHOT BY A WHITE MAN" in the New-York Tribune and "WELL DUNN" in the Chicago Tribune. The Sun's fuller report, headed "ATTACKED BY A CROWD OF NEGROES," praised Dunn's "coolness" and quoted his old colonel calling him an excellent soldier.

Summaries garbled the details, calling Dunn a policeman, placing the town in North Carolina, or counting three dead. The Bristol News treated it as a holiday curiosity, remarking that "three negro corpses" from one man "would seem to imply a fair amount of whiskey." Guffin's letter in the Chicago Tribune was the only item found that condemned the killings, calling Dunn a "double murderer" and the trial a "sham."

The wire and Fortress Monroe accounts, which Dunn's friends echoed, presented the killings as self-defence against men who attacked him. Guffin, who said he attended the trial, wrote instead that Dunn was drunk and that there was "not even the slightest cause or provocation." Some briefs reported three dead, while Guffin's later letter counted two killed and one wounded.

reader.title: Smithville shooting (1880)
bases: A single white man, Howard Dunn, shot two Black men dead and stabbed others at a gathering of Black men; no white mob, band or officers took part (A2, A18, A57).

The Fort Monroe wire dispatch (A2), the fuller Fortress Monroe report (A18), the Clarke Courier trial item (A56) and an eyewitness letter from Yorktown (A57) agree that Dunn killed two Black men at Smithville on Christmas Eve, though they disagree on provocation.

accounts.label: Fort Monroe wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A Black man pulled Dunn's whiskers and slapped him; Dunn shot him, reloaded in a store, shot Cook when the crowd attacked with a sword, and cut his way out.

accounts.label: Fuller Fortress Monroe report
accounts.gist: Drinking men chaffed Dunn over his no-hunting notices and sought a fight; Dunn shot his assailant, then Cook, and escaped; his friends claimed self-defence.

accounts.label: Yorktown eyewitness letter
accounts.gist: A drunken Dunn killed two "innocent" men without provocation and was acquitted on appeals to race and Confederate service.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Fort Monroe dispatch under headlines like "Desperate Affray on the Peninsula" and "FATAL AFFRAY."
The Sun headed its fuller report "ATTACKED BY A CROWD OF NEGROES" and praised Dunn's "coolness."
The Chicago Tribune ran the dispatch under the pun "WELL DUNN" but later printed Guffin's letter condemning the acquittal.
Guffin called the trial "sham" and Dunn a "double murderer."
